This is interesting, don't see many no boil beers on here, can you post the recipe?

Sure! 3 gallon batch. 2lbs CMC pale malt, 2lbs Briess white wheat. OG 1.033. Mash at 148F for an hour. I added about 4 cascade hop pellets to the mash. I did BIAB for this so I just lifted the bag out, drained it and then heated it up to 170F for a minute or so to kill off anything in the wort. Chilled to 100F and tossed in half a container of Good Belly for 48hrs. Chilled to 64F and pitched a 500mL starter of Conan. I'll let it ferment out and the add ~5lbs raspberries.

I am always skeptical of studies in economics ever since my macro and microeconomics classes in college. People try to pass it off as some sort of a science but it is nothing more than a best guess field. People can predict what will happen all they want but they are just guessing. Economics is too driven by people (as opposed to nature) to be exact. I would bet you money I can find a study that a different economist did that says the exact opposite of this study.

We won't really know unless it happens and even then it will take months or years before there is enough data to know the full impact.

I'm for incremental minimum wage increases. The one thing I have to give them is that sudden large increases will cost jobs. The general premise is that businesses will see the money return as people spend more, but that still requires some time while people pay-off debt before treating the new income as expendable. Suddenly shocking the system with a potential doubling of employee expenses means that some businesses that run on marginal profits (or sometimes losses for businesses that are seasonal), like many restaurants/bars, will be forced to either shut their doors, or push deep into the red with payroll loans (assuming that they can get them) until consumer spending increases to the point where they are profitable again.

There are some points in the article that are pretty detached from reality though. In most companies I know, employee productivity is pushed to the limit before they even think about hiring another employee. If they need another employee to meet production demands (if they can't get more product out, they can't increase profits) then they need another person regardless if the minimum wage is $7.50, $10, or $15. So assuming that they'll just "ask their employees to be more productive" is just backwards.

Also automation of jobs is a thing that will happen regardless of the minimum wage. If there is a program or robot that can replace an employee, that employee will eventually be replaced.
